# 01 — Architecture & Installation of RHEL 9

**Duration: 2 hours · 3 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐**

## Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you will know:
- Describe the complete boot sequence (firmware → GRUB2 → kernel → systemd)
- Understand why initramfs exists and what it contains
- Create and validate a Kickstart file for automated installation
- Manage Red Hat subscriptions with `subscription-manager`
- Recover a system in rescue mode

## Why this chapter is fundamental

Any SRE who does not understand how to start their machine **works blindly**. When a server refuses to start at 3 a.m., there's no GUI or fancy tools — just your knowledge of what happens between the power button and the login.

## The startup sequence

```
Alimentation électrique
        │
        ▼
Firmware (BIOS legacy ou UEFI)
    │   Initialise le matériel (RAM, bus PCI, disques)
    │   Cherche un boot device
        │
        ▼
GRUB2 — Grand Unified Bootloader version 2
    │   Charge le kernel Linux en mémoire
    │   Lit /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
        │
        ▼
Kernel Linux (vmlinuz-5.14.x-xxx.el9.x86_64)
    │   Monte l'initramfs (mini système en RAM)
    │   Monte le vrai système de fichiers racine
    │   Lance systemd (PID 1)
        │
        ▼
systemd (PID 1)
    │   Démarre tous les services dans l'ordre
    │   Active les targets (multi-user, graphical...)
        │
        ▼
Login prompt
```

## Initramfs: why does it exist?

> **The initramfs paradox**: the kernel needs the disk drivers to mount the disk — but the drivers are on the disk that it cannot yet read.

**The solution:** the initramfs is a mini-image (compressed cpio archive) loaded directly into RAM by GRUB. It contains storage drivers, LUKS tools, RAID tools, and a troubleshooting shell.

```bash
# Inspecter le contenu de votre initramfs
lsinitrd /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img | head -50

# Sa taille (généralement 20-40 Mo)
ls -lh /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img
```

## GRUB2 — Absolute rule

> Never modify `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` directly. It is generated automatically. Always go through `/etc/default/grub` + `grub2-mkconfig`.

```bash
# Modifier la configuration
vim /etc/default/grub

# Régénérer (BIOS)
grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

# Régénérer (UEFI)
grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/grub.cfg
```

- **Lab 01**: Analyze the boot sequence with `systemd-analyze`
- **Lab 02**: Create a Kickstart file and validate with `ksvalidator`
- **Lab 03**: Recover a forgotten root password via `rd.break`

03-systemd-services.contentEn:
#03 — Systemd & Services

**Duration: 2 hours · 4 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐**

## Systemd: the manager of everything

Systemd is PID 1. It manages services, mounts, timers, sockets, and targets (replacements for SysV runlevels).

```bash
# Les commandes essentielles
systemctl status nginx
systemctl start|stop|restart|reload nginx
systemctl enable|disable nginx    # au démarrage
systemctl mask nginx              # empêcher tout démarrage

# Voir les dépendances
systemctl list-dependencies nginx

# Analyser le temps de démarrage
systemd-analyze blame | head -20
systemd-analyze critical-chain
```

## Create a custom systemd service

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/mon-app.service
[Unit]
Description=Mon Application
After=network.target postgresql.service
Requires=postgresql.service

[Service]
Type=exec
User=appuser
WorkingDirectory=/opt/mon-app
ExecStart=/opt/mon-app/bin/start.sh
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=mon-app

# Sécurité
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```bash
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now mon-app
journalctl -u mon-app -f  # suivre les logs en direct
```

04-stockage-lvm-stratis.contentEn:
#04 — Advanced Storage: LVM & Stratis

**Duration: 3 hours · 5 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐⭐**

Dense chapter. LVM is essential in production. Stratis is the new RHEL 8/9.

## LVM in 3 layers

```
Disques physiques (sda, sdb, nvme0n1...)
        │ pvcreate
        ▼
Physical Volumes (PV)
        │ vgcreate
        ▼
Volume Groups (VG) — le pool
        │ lvcreate
        ▼
Logical Volumes (LV) — les "disques virtuels"
        │ mkfs + mount
        ▼
Système de fichiers (ext4, xfs...)
```

```bash
# Créer un LVM complet
pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
lvcreate -L 50G -n lv_app vg_data
mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_app
mount /dev/vg_data/lv_app /data

# Étendre en ligne (sans démonter !)
lvextend -L +20G /dev/vg_data/lv_app
xfs_growfs /data  # XFS s'étend en ligne
```

> **SRE use case**: disk full at 3 a.m. LVM allows you to add a disk and extend the filesystem in less than 2 minutes, without downtime.

06-selinux.contentEn:
#06 — SELinux — Mandatory Security

**Duration: 2h30 · 4 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐⭐**

## Why SELinux is fundamental (and misunderstood)

Most tutorials say "if that doesn't work, do `setenforce 0`". This is a serious error. With SELinux Enforcing, a compromised web server remains **confined** in its `httpd_t` domain — it cannot access `/etc/shadow`, SSH keys, other services.

> **SELinux is not an obstacle, it is your safety net.**

## DAC vs MAC

```bash
# DAC (permissions UNIX) : le propriétaire décide
ls -la /var/www/html/  # root peut tout faire

# MAC (SELinux) : la politique système décide
# Même root ne peut pas sortir de son domaine SELinux
getenforce  # Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled
sestatus    # informations complètes
```

## Read a AVC message

```
type=AVC msg=audit(1705324800.123:456): avc: denied
  { read write }           ← opérations refusées
  for pid=1234
  comm="nginx"             ← processus
  path="/srv/monsite/"     ← ressource
  scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0     ← SOURCE
  tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0  ← CIBLE
```

**Quick reading:** nginx (`httpd_t`) wants to read a file with type `user_home_t`. Solution: change the context of the file.

## The 6-step solution method

```
1. setenforce 0  → Permissive pour diagnostiquer
2. Reproduire le problème
3. ausearch -m avc -ts recent
4. sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log
5. Appliquer la bonne solution
6. setenforce 1  → Repasser en Enforcing
```

## The three solutions

```bash
# Solution A — Mauvais contexte de fichier (le plus fréquent)
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/monsite(/.*)?" 
restorecon -Rv /srv/monsite/

# Solution B — Boolean SELinux
getsebool -a | grep httpd
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on

# Solution C — Module personnalisé (dernier recours)
audit2allow -M mon-module < /var/log/audit/audit.log
semodule -i mon-module.pp
```

07-podman-conteneurs.contentEn:
# 07 — Podman & Containers on RHEL 9

**Duration: 2 hours · 3 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐**

## Podman vs Docker — the operational difference

Podman does not have a daemon. Each container is a direct child process of the podman command. Consequences:

- No root daemon needed → rootless containers by default
- If the server restarts, the containers do not restart automatically (→ use `systemd`)
- Compatible with Docker images (same OCI format)

```bash
# Docker → Podman : drop-in replacement
alias docker=podman

# Rootless container
podman run -d --name nginx -p 8080:80 nginx

# Générer un service systemd depuis un conteneur
podman generate systemd --new --name nginx > ~/.config/systemd/user/nginx.service
systemctl --user enable --now nginx
```

## Full content on Gumroad

Podman Compose, custom images, private registries, systemd integration, Podman pods (Kubernetes Pods equivalent).

#08 — Ansible on RHEL 9

**Duration: 3 hours · 5 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐**

## Ansible for RHEL SREs

Ansible is the reference configuration tool as code on RHEL. Red Hat acquired it in 2015 and it is deeply integrated into the RHEL ecosystem.

```yaml
# Playbook type : configuration d'un serveur RHEL 9
---
- name: Configurer un serveur web RHEL 9
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes

  vars:
    app_port: 8080
    app_user: appuser

  tasks:
    - name: Installer les paquets nécessaires
      dnf:
        name:
          - nginx
          - python3
          - firewalld
        state: present

    - name: Configurer SELinux pour le port custom
      seport:
        ports: "{{ app_port }}"
        proto: tcp
        setype: http_port_t
        state: present

    - name: Ouvrir le port dans firewalld
      firewalld:
        port: "{{ app_port }}/tcp"
        permanent: yes
        state: enabled
        immediate: yes

    - name: Démarrer nginx
      systemd:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: yes
```

#11 — Advanced Bash Scripting

**Duration: 2 hours · 3 labs · Level ⭐⭐⭐**

## SRE patterns in Bash

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail  # Toujours. Toujours.

# Logging structuré
log() { echo "[$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S)] $*" >&2; }
error() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

# Cleanup automatique
trap 'log "Script interrompu"; cleanup' EXIT INT TERM

cleanup() {
  rm -f /tmp/mon_script_*.tmp
}

# Retry avec backoff exponentiel
retry() {
  local max_attempts=$1; shift
  local attempt=1
  until "$@"; do
    [[ $attempt -ge $max_attempts ]] && error "Échec après $attempt tentatives"
    log "Tentative $attempt/$max_attempts échouée. Retry dans $((attempt * 2))s..."
    sleep $((attempt * 2))
    ((attempt++))
  done
}

# Usage
retry 5 curl -sf https://api.example.com/health
```

# Part 1 — Linux & Systems

20 questions · Level: Fundamental → Senior

---

**Q1. What is an inode?**

An inode is a container of a file's metadata: permissions, ownership, timestamps, size, and especially pointers to the data blocks on disk. The file name is *not* in the inode — it's in the directory (which is itself a special file).

```bash
stat fichier.txt              # voir l'inode et ses métadonnées
ls -i fichier.txt             # numéro d'inode
df -i                         # inodes utilisés/libres par filesystem
find / -inum 123456           # trouver un fichier par son inode
```

**Maintenance trap:** "Your disk has free space but you can no longer create files. Why?"
Answer: Inodes are exhausted. `df -i` will confirm this.

---

**Q2. Process vs. Thread — what's the difference?**

| | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|  
| Memory | Separate space | Shared with parent process |
| Creation | Slow (`fork()`) | Fast |
| Insulation | Total | Partial (shared memory access) |
| Communication | IPC (pipes, sockets) | Shared variables |

```bash
# Voir les threads d'un processus
ps -eLf | grep nginx
top -H -p PID    # -H = afficher les threads
```

---

**Q3. What is a zombie process?**

A zombie is a process that has finished executing but whose entry has not yet been cleaned up in the process table. He is dead but his PID is still busy.

**Cause:** the parent process did not call `wait()` to retrieve the return code of its child.

```bash
ps aux | grep Z    # Z = zombie
# Zombies en grand nombre = bug dans l'application parente
# Solution : tuer le processus parent (il sera réadopté par systemd qui appellera wait())
```

---

**Q4. OOM Killer — how does he choose his victim?**

When RAM is exhausted, the kernel calculates an `oom_score` for each process (0-1000). The process with the highest score is killed.

```bash
# Voir le score d'un processus
cat /proc/$(pgrep nginx)/oom_score

# Protéger un processus critique (valeur -1000 = immunisé)
echo -1000 > /proc/$(pgrep postgresql)/oom_score_adj

# Voir les OOM kills récents
dmesg | grep -i "oom kill"
grep -i "out of memory" /var/log/messages
```

---

**Q5. Load average vs CPU usage — what’s the difference?**

- **CPU usage**: % of CPU time used
- **Load average**: average number of processes waiting for execution OR waiting for I/O

A CPU at 100% with load average at 1.0 is normal (a CPU-bound process).
A CPU at 5% with load average at 10.0 is an I/O problem (slow disk or network).

```bash
uptime                 # load average 1m, 5m, 15m
# Interpréter : diviser par le nb de CPUs
# Load/CPUs < 1 : pas saturé
# Load/CPUs > 1 : saturé
nproc                  # nombre de CPUs
```

---

*Questions 6-20 available in the full guide on Gumroad.*

**Topics covered in Q6-Q20:** cgroups, namespaces, file descriptors, swap vs RAM, Kubernetes and swap, `top` vs `htop`, orphaned processes, Linux signals (SIGKILL vs SIGTERM), ulimits, and `/proc` filesystem.

partie-2-kubernetes.contentEn:
# Part 2 — Kubernetes

25 questions · Level: Junior → Senior SRE

---

**Q21. Explain the flow of a `kubectl apply` to the running Pod.**

```
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
        │
        ▼
API Server (validation + authentification + admission controllers)
        │
        ▼
etcd (stockage de l'état désiré)
        │
        ▼
Scheduler (choisit le node : resources, affinités, taints)
        │
        ▼
kubelet (sur le node choisi)
        │ télécharge l'image (si pas en cache)
        ▼
containerd (runtime) → Pod en Running
        │
        ▼
kube-proxy (met à jour les règles iptables/ipvs pour les Services)
```

**Classic follow-up question:** “What could be blocking each step?”
- API Server: insufficient RBAC, quota exceeded, admission controller blocking
- Scheduler: not enough resources, taints without tolerance, nodeSelector does not match
- kubelet: image not found (ImagePullBackOff), memory limits too low

---

**Q22. What is the difference between Liveness and Readiness probe?**

| | Liveness | Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | “Is the container alive?” | “Can it receive traffic?” |
| Action if failure | Container restart | Removal of the Service (no traffic) |
| Use cases | Detecting a deadlock | Wait for the app to be ready |

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 30  # temps de démarrage
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
```

---

**Q23. Requests vs Limits — what happens if an app exceeds its limits?**

- **CPU limit exceeded**: throttling (the process is slowed down) — never killed
- **Memory limit exceeded**: OOMKilled (the container is killed immediately)

```bash
# Voir les OOMKilled
kubectl describe pod mypod | grep -A5 "Last State"
# Output: Reason: OOMKilled

# Voir l'utilisation actuelle
kubectl top pods --containers
```

**Interview advice:** do not confuse "requests" (guaranteed by the scheduler) and "limits" (maximum authorized).

---

# Part 3 — CI/CD & IaC

25 questions · GitLab CI, Terraform, Ansible

---

**Q46. What is idempotence and why is it critical in IaC?**

An operation is idempotent if applying it once or ten times produces the same end result. In IaC, it is the fundamental property that makes tools reliable.

```yaml
# Ansible — idempotent
- name: Créer l'utilisateur
  user:
    name: appuser
    state: present  # si existe déjà → rien ne change

# Script bash — PAS idempotent
- name: Créer l'utilisateur
  command: useradd appuser  # échoue si existe déjà
```

Terraform is designed for idempotence: `terraform apply` multiple times = same infrastructure.

---

**Q47. Terraform state — why is it a critical component?**

The state is Terraform's "source of truth" on the real state of your infrastructure. Without it, Terraform doesn't know what it has already created.

```hcl
# Backend S3 + DynamoDB (verrouillage)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "mon-bucket-tfstate"
    key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-lock"
  }
}
```

**Maintenance pitfalls:**
- "What happens if two people do `terraform apply` at the same time?" → race condition → DynamoDB lock
- “How to recover after state corruption?” → `terraform state` commands, backup S3

---

# Part 4 — Observability

20 questions · Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tracing

---

**Q71. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?**

- **Monitoring**: answer *pre-defined* questions (“CPU > 80%?”)
- **Observability**: answer *ad-hoc* questions ("why is this query slow for this user?")

With monitoring alone, you know THAT something is broken. With observability, you understand WHY.

---

**Q72. Explain the Prometheus data model.**

Prometheus stores **time series**: each series is identified by a metric name and a set of labels.

```
http_requests_total{method="GET", status="200", service="api"} 1234
        │                    │                                    │
   nom métrique           labels                               valeur
```

**The 4 types of metrics:**
- `Counter`: can only increase (requests, errors)
- `Gauge`: can go up/down (CPU, memory)
- `Histogram`: distribution of values (latencies in buckets)
- `Summary`: quantiles calculated on the application side

```promql
# Taux de requêtes par seconde (5 dernières minutes)
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Latence p99
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# Error rate
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])
```

#01 — Docker Architecture & Installation

**Level ⭐⭐ · 2h · 2 labs**

## Internal architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│     Docker Client (CLI)             │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────┘
               │ Docker API
┌──────────────▼──────────────────────┐
│        Docker Daemon (dockerd)      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │   Container Runtime          │   │
│  │   (containerd, runc)         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
┌──────────────▼──────────────────────┐
│      Système d'exploitation hôte    │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key components:**
- `dockerd`: the daemon (server)
- `containerd`: high-level container runtime
- `runc`: low-level runtime (creates Linux namespaces)
- Docker Client: the CLI you use

## Docker vs VMs — the real difference

| | VMs | Docker |
|---|---|---|
| Insulation | Full hypervisor | Linux Namespaces |
| Size | Several GB | A few MB |
| Getting Started | Minutes | Seconds |
| Guest OS | Complete | Shared with host |

## Installation (Linux)

```bash
# Ubuntu/Debian
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-compose-plugin

# Ajouter ton user au groupe docker
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Activer au démarrage
sudo systemctl enable docker
```

## Daemon configuration

```json
// /etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" },
  "storage-driver": "overlay2",
  "default-ulimits": { "nofile": { "Name": "nofile", "Hard": 64000, "Soft": 64000 } }
}
```

#03 — Dockerfile Advanced & Multi-stage Builds

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 3h · 3 labs**

## Production Dockerfile — all instructions

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM node:18-alpine AS base

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="Mon App"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="1.0.0"

ARG NODE_ENV=production
ENV NODE_ENV=${NODE_ENV} PORT=3000

WORKDIR /app

# Copier les dépendances D'ABORD (cache layers)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production && npm cache clean --force

COPY . .

# Utilisateur non-root
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodejs && adduser -S nodejs -u 1001
RUN chown -R nodejs:nodejs /app
USER nodejs

EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -q --spider http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["node"]
CMD ["server.js"]
```

## Multi-stage builds — reduce size by 10x

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 : Build
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2 : Test (optionnel)
FROM builder AS test
RUN npm run test

# Stage 3 : Production — seulement ce qui est nécessaire
FROM node:18-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

## BuildKit — cache mounts and secrets

```dockerfile
# Cache npm entre les builds
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --only=production

# Secret au build (ne reste PAS dans l'image finale)
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token)" > .npmrc && \
    npm install && rm .npmrc
```

```bash
# Build avec secret
docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=.npm_token -t mon-app .
```

## ADD vs COPY, ENTRYPOINT vs CMD

```dockerfile
# COPY : toujours préférer à ADD (sauf décompression d'archive)
COPY fichier.txt /app/
ADD archive.tar.gz /app/  # décompresse automatiquement

# ENTRYPOINT : commande fixe
# CMD : arguments par défaut (facile à override)
ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
CMD ["app.py"]
# → python app.py
# Override : docker run mon-image script.py → python script.py
```

#06 — Docker Security

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 2h · 2 labs**

## The 6 security principles

### 1. Non-root user (required in prod)

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodejs && \
    adduser -S nodejs -u 1001 && \
    chown -R nodejs:nodejs /app
USER nodejs  # JAMAIS root en production
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

### 2. Official and slim images

```dockerfile
FROM node:18.17.0-alpine  # ✓ Version exacte, image minimale
# FROM node:latest          # ✗ Imprévisible
# FROM ubuntu               # ✗ Surface d'attaque trop large
```

### 3. Vulnerability scanning

```bash
# Docker Scout (intégré depuis Docker 4.17)
docker scout cves mon-image:latest
docker scout recommendations mon-image:latest

# Trivy (open source, recommandé en CI)
trivy image mon-image:latest
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL mon-image:latest

# Snyk
snyk container test mon-image:latest
```

### 4. Limit resources and capabilities

```bash
# Limites mémoire/CPU
docker run -m 512m --cpus="1.5" --pids-limit=100 mon-image

# Filesystem read-only
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp mon-image

# Supprimer toutes les capabilities, n'ajouter que le nécessaire
docker run --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE mon-image

# Pas de nouveaux privilèges
docker run --security-opt=no-new-privileges mon-image
```

### 5. Secrets management

```bash
# NE PAS faire ça (visible dans docker inspect)
docker run -e DB_PASSWORD=motdepasse mon-image  # ✗

# Préférer un fichier .env (non versionné)
docker run --env-file .env mon-image  # ✓

# Ou Docker Secrets (Swarm)
echo "mot_de_passe" | docker secret create db_password -
```

### 6. Content Trust (image signing)

```bash
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
docker trust sign registry.example.com/mon-app:latest
docker trust inspect registry.example.com/mon-app:latest
```

## Security checklist before pushing into production

- [ ] Alpine or slim image (not ubuntu/debian full)
- [ ] Non-root user in Dockerfile
- [ ] `--read-only` filesystem if possible
- [ ] `--cap-drop=ALL` + minimum capabilities
- [ ] Scan Trivy: zero HIGH/CRITICAL not fixed
- [ ] Secrets via .env file or Docker Secrets (never in the Dockerfile)
- [ ] Memory and CPU limit set

# 07 — Optimization & Best Practices

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 2h · 2 labs**

## Reduce image size

**Rule #1: order of cache instructions**

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Les dépendances changent rarement → en premier (mise en cache)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Le code source change souvent → en dernier

CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

**Rule #2: Single Coat for Installations**

```dockerfile
# ✗ 2 couches
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# ✓ 1 couche
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y curl && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

```
node_modules
npm-debug.log

dist
coverage

Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
```

#01 — Kubernetes Introduction & Architecture

**Level ⭐ · 2h · 1 lab**

## What is Kubernetes?

Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform created by Google in 2014, donated to the CNCF in 2015. It automates the deployment, scaling and management of containerized applications.

> K8s shines for complex distributed applications. It is **not recommended** for small, simple apps — the operational cost is real.

## Architecture: Control Plane + Worker Nodes

```
┌─────────────────── CONTROL PLANE ──────────────────────┐
│                                                         │
│  kube-apiserver  ←  point d'entrée de toutes les req.  │
│  etcd            ←  base de données du cluster          │
│  kube-scheduler  ←  assigne les pods aux nodes          │
│  kube-controller-manager  ←  maintient l'état désiré   │
│                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
             │  API
┌────────────▼────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  WORKER NODES (1..N)                    │
│                                                         │
│  kubelet        ←  agent sur chaque node                │
│  kube-proxy     ←  règles réseau (iptables/ipvs)        │
│  containerd     ←  container runtime                    │
│                                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## History

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 2014 | First public release (based on Borg from Google) |
| 2015 | Donation to the CNCF, version 1.0 |
| 2016+ | De facto standard — mass adoption |
| 2026 | >80% of Fortune 500 companies use it |

# 02 — Fundamental Concepts: Pod, Deployment, Service

**Level ⭐⭐ · 3h · 3 labs**

## Pod — minimum unit

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mon-pod
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    resources:
      requests: { memory: "64Mi", cpu: "250m" }
      limits: { memory: "128Mi", cpu: "500m" }
```

> A Pod = 1 or more containers that share network and storage. In practice: 1 Pod = 1 main container.

## Deployment — manage a set of pods

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mon-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: mon-app }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: mon-app }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
```

## Service — stably expose pods

| Type | Usage |
|---|---|
| **ClusterIP** | Internal communication (default) |
| **NodePort** | External exposure via node port |
| **LoadBalancer** | External load balancer (cloud) |
| **ExternalName** | External DNS Redirection |

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mon-service
spec:
  selector: { app: mon-app }
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
```

## Why labels are critical

```bash
# Labels permettent de sélectionner des groupes de ressources
kubectl get pods -l app=mon-app
kubectl get pods -l environment=production,tier=frontend
kubectl delete pods -l environment=test  # Attention !
```

- **Lab 02**: Create a Deployment 3 replicas, kill a pod and observe the automatic recreation
- **Lab 03**: Expose the Deployment with a NodePort Service, access via browser

# 03 — kubectl: Essential Commands & Debugging

**Level ⭐⭐ · 2h · 3 labs**

## Everyday orders

```bash
# Créer / appliquer
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f ./mon-dossier/  # tous les fichiers YAML

# Lister / décrire
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -o wide          # avec node et IP
kubectl get all -n production     # tout dans un namespace
kubectl describe pod mon-pod      # détails complets
kubectl get pod mon-pod -o yaml   # YAML complet

# Modifier
kubectl edit deployment mon-deployment
kubectl scale deployment mon-app --replicas=5
kubectl set image deployment/mon-app nginx=nginx:1.26

# Supprimer
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
kubectl delete pod mon-pod
```

## Debugging — commands that save

```bash
# Logs
kubectl logs mon-pod
kubectl logs -f mon-pod                    # suivre en temps réel
kubectl logs mon-pod -c mon-conteneur      # conteneur spécifique
kubectl logs --previous mon-pod            # logs du conteneur précédent (après crash)

# Exec dans un pod
kubectl exec -it mon-pod -- /bin/bash
kubectl exec -it mon-pod -- curl localhost:8080/health

# Port-forwarding
kubectl port-forward service/mon-service 8080:80
kubectl port-forward pod/mon-pod 8080:3000

# Debug avec un pod temporaire
kubectl run debug --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh
```

## Rollouts — version management

```bash
kubectl rollout status deployment/mon-app
kubectl rollout history deployment/mon-app
kubectl rollout undo deployment/mon-app             # version précédente
kubectl rollout undo deployment/mon-app --to-revision=2  # version spécifique
```

## Contexts and namespaces

```bash
# Changer de contexte (cluster)
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context mon-cluster

# Namespace par défaut pour la session
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=production

# Astuce : alias utiles
alias k=kubectl
alias kgp='kubectl get pods'
alias kdp='kubectl describe pod'
alias klog='kubectl logs -f'
```

# 05 — Advanced Concepts: Namespaces, Volumes, RBAC

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 3h · 3 labs**

## Namespaces — logical isolation

```bash
# Créer des namespaces par environnement
kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl create namespace staging
kubectl create namespace production

# Travailler dans un namespace
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -n production
kubectl get pods -n production
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
```

## PersistentVolumes (PV) and PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC)

```yaml
# PersistentVolumeClaim
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
  storageClassName: standard
```

```yaml
# Utiliser le PVC dans un Pod
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: postgres-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: postgres-pvc
  containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: postgres:15
    volumeMounts:
    - name: postgres-storage
      mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
```

## RBAC — who can do what

```yaml
# Role (dans un namespace)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
```

```yaml
# RoleBinding — lier un Role à un utilisateur
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

```bash
# Vérifier les permissions
kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace=production --as=alice
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace=production --as=alice
```

## Network Policies

```yaml
# Autoriser uniquement le trafic du frontend vers le backend
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: backend }
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: frontend }
    ports:
    - port: 8080
```

- **Lab 03**: RBAC — create a user who can read pods in production but not delete them

06-strategies-deploiement.contentEn:
#06 — Deployment Strategies

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 2h · 2 labs**

## Rolling Update (default) — zero downtime

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1         # pods supplémentaires pendant la MàJ
    maxUnavailable: 0   # zéro pod indisponible à tout moment
```

Principle: K8s creates a new pod, waits for it to be `Ready`, then deletes an old one. Repeat until the end.

## Recreate — simple but with downtime

```yaml
strategy:
  type: Recreate
```

Deletes all old pods, then creates new ones. Use case: applications that do not support 2 versions in parallel (DB schema migration without backward compat).

## Blue-Green — instant switch

```bash
# Deployer la version Green à côté de Blue
kubectl apply -f deployment-green.yaml  # version v2

# Quand Green est prêt, basculer le Service
kubectl patch service mon-service \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'

# Rollback : re-patch vers blue
kubectl patch service mon-service \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'
```

Advantage: instant rollback. Disadvantage: Doubles resources during transition.

## Canary — progressive validation

```bash
# Déployer 10% sur la nouvelle version (1 pod sur 10)
# stable: 9 réplicas, canary: 1 réplica
kubectl apply -f deployment-stable.yaml    # 9 réplicas, version v1
kubectl apply -f deployment-canary.yaml   # 1 réplica, version v2

# Le Service sélectionne les deux versions (via label commun)
# → 10% du trafic va vers canary

# Si OK, augmenter progressivement
kubectl scale deployment canary --replicas=5   # 50%
kubectl scale deployment canary --replicas=10  # 100%
kubectl delete deployment stable
```

## PodDisruptionBudget — protect availability

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: mon-app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2  # au moins 2 pods disponibles à tout moment
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: mon-app }
```

Essential for managed clusters with node maintenance: prevents K8s from draining a node if this would create an outage.

# 07 — Monitoring, Observability & Best Practices

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 2h · 1 lab**

## Metrics with Metrics Server

```bash
# Installer
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

# Utilisation des ressources en temps réel
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods
kubectl top pods --sort-by=memory -n production
```

## Stack Prometheus + Grafana

Recommended deployment via kube-prometheus-stack (Helm):

```bash
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm install kube-prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace
```

What we have with kube-prometheus-stack:
- Prometheus (automatic scrape of nodes, pods, and annotated services)
- Grafana (ready-to-use K8s dashboards)
- AlertManager (PagerDuty, Slack, email)
- kube-state-metrics + node-exporter

## Centralized logging — Loki

```bash
helm install loki grafana/loki-stack \
  --namespace monitoring \
  --set grafana.enabled=false \
  --set promtail.enabled=true
```

Promtail automatically collects logs from all pods → Loki → Grafana.

## Best practices — prod checklist

**Organization:**
- Namespaces by environment (dev/staging/prod)
- Consistent labels on all resources
- Annotations for documentation

**Configuration:**
- Always set `requests` and `limits` on containers
- ConfigMaps for config, Secrets for sensitive data
- Never the `latest` tag in production

**Security:**
- RBAC enabled, principle of least privilege
- Network Policies to isolate namespaces
- Scan images with Trivy before deployment
- SecurityContext: `runAsNonRoot: true`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`

**High availability:**
- Minimum 3 replicas for critical services
- PodDisruptionBudget on all prod Deployments
- Anti-affinity rules to distribute across multiple nodes
- Regular etcd backup

```yaml
# SecurityContext recommandé
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1001
    fsGroup: 2000
  containers:
  - name: app
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: [ALL]
```

#08 — Rancher & Multi-Cluster Management

**Level ⭐⭐⭐ · 3h · 2 labs**

## What is Rancher?

Rancher (Rancher Labs / SUSE) is a Kubernetes cluster management platform. It unifies the management of multiple clusters in a single interface — no matter if they are on EKS, AKS, GKE, RKE2, or bare-metal.

**Typical use case:** a platform with a production cluster, staging, and several client clusters. Without Rancher, you juggle between 5 kubeconfig files. With Rancher, only one UI.

## Rancher Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            Rancher Server                   │
│   (management cluster: K3s ou RKE2 interne) │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                     │
         ┌───────────┴────────────┐
         ▼                        ▼
┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐
│  Cluster Prod   │    │  Cluster Staging    │
│  (RKE2/EKS)    │    │  (K3s/AKS)          │
│  Rancher Agent  │    │  Rancher Agent      │
└─────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘
```

## Rancher installation (Helm, production)

```bash
# Namespace + cert-manager
kubectl create namespace cattle-system
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.13.0/cert-manager.yaml

# Rancher avec Let's Encrypt
helm repo add rancher-latest https://releases.rancher.com/server-charts/latest
helm install rancher rancher-latest/rancher \
  --namespace cattle-system \
  --set hostname=rancher.example.com \
  --set bootstrapPassword=admin \
  --set ingress.tls.source=letsEncrypt \
  --set letsEncrypt.email=admin@example.com

kubectl -n cattle-system rollout status deploy/rancher
```

## Quick installation (Dev/Test)

```bash
docker run -d --restart=unless-stopped \
  -p 80:80 -p 443:443 \
  --privileged \
  rancher/rancher:latest
```

## Multi-cluster management

```bash
# Via Rancher CLI
rancher clusters ls
rancher kubectl config use-context mon-cluster

# Importer un cluster existant
# UI : Cluster Management > Import Existing > copier la commande
kubectl apply -f https://rancher.example.com/v3/import/xxxxx.yaml
```

## Cluster types

| Type | Description | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| **RKE2** | Distribution Rancher, FIPS compliant | Enterprise production |
| **K3s** | Lightweight < 100MB, arm compatible | Edge, IoT, dev |
| **EKS/AKS/GKE** | Imported Managed Cloud | Multi-cloud |

## Centralized RBAC in Rancher

- **Global Roles**: Admin, Standard User
- **Cluster Roles**: Cluster Owner, Cluster Member
- **Project Roles**: Project Owner, Read-only

Rancher projects group together multiple namespaces — useful for organizing a team's workloads without creating a cluster per team.

## Kubernetes ecosystem — essential tools

| Tool | Category | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Helm** | Package manager | Deploy complex apps with one command |
| **Kustomize** | Config management | YAML patches without templates |
| **ArgoCD** | GitOps | Git synchronization → continuous cluster |
| **K9s** | Terminal UI | Explore and manage the cluster without remembering commands |
| **Lens** | IDE | Complete GUI |
| **Istio** | Mesh service | Traffic management, mTLS, observability |
